text.p: On overnight commodity markets, the gold price edged slightly higher, while copper bounced a touch on technical factors.
Oil prices settled lower on news the German government would sell its oil reserves.
Wheat prices fell again on good U.S. harvest news.
The CRB index fell 1.19 points to 232.70.
Technical rallies in the LME base metal complex ran out of steam during late Thursday trading, and contracts finished mixed.

Analysts said that the initial rallies, which were led by copper, reflected the sell-offs seen this week attracting some Far Eastern buying interest, which then trigered short-covereing. But business was not particularly active.

Traders said levels of $2,230 on Wednesday - a 4-1/2 month low - were the springboard for a technical correction. But the rally faded, as expected, near $2,295/2,300. Last trade was at $2,268, still up $32 from Wednesday's kerb.
Aluminium tended to mirror copper, and was unable to wade through the resistance above $1,580. By the kerb prices were just $2 higher at $1,570.

May IPAI producer inventory data was mixed, with total stocks down, but unwrought up, and thus had little impact on sentiment. Another one-day strike at Spanish producer Inespal also had little affect, traders said.
Nickel again fell back during the afternoon sessions, having encountered overhead resistance above $6,900.
Also, stocks are seen rising in coming weeks, despite today's decrease, given talk of ample Russian availability. Last trade was at $6,850, down $40.
Zinc eased back from the resistance above $1,480, but still ended higher, reflecting the narrowing contango and increasing tightness in September.
Last three months business was at $1,479, a $15 gain from Wednesday, with the market expected to re-test last week's 6-3/4 year highs of $1,495 soon.
NYMEX crude settled lower Thursday on news the German government would sell 400 million marks ($230 million) worth of oil to cut its widening budget deficit and will sell more oil in 1998.

Dealers said Germany's sales will add 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) to the market for the remainder of this year and comes on top of the anticipated resumption of Iraqi oil sales. August crude ended 24 cents a barrel lower at $19.22.
The market pushed August crude as far down as $19.07, its lowest level since June 26, upon hearing Germany will sell oil from its strategic reserves.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mostly higher Thursday, with gold, silver and even platinum recovering some ground and only palladium ending lower after confirmation Russian metal exports to Japan resumed after a six-month suspension.
COMEX August gold ended up $1.90 at $320.80 an ounce after gapping higher on the open and then consolidating for most of the day. The August/December spread ended steady around $3.60.
In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted at $319.60/$320.10 at the close compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix of $319.80 and the New York close Wednesday of $318.00/50.
Gold fixed at a 12-year low early Wednesday of $315.75 in London in the wake of last week's decision of Australian central bank to sell 167 tonnes of gold.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed lower on harvest pressure including hedge selling and news that Egypt would not be in the market soon for U.S. wheat, traders said. Only minor delays to wheat combining were reported this week in key U.S.

Winter wheat areas and the market was expecting Friday's USDA wheat production report to show a large production number for the U.S. An average of analysts' estimates ahead of the report pegged 1997 U.S. winter wheat production at 1.687 billion bushels, above the output last year at 1.478 billion.
Analysts said favorable growing weather after a spring freeze in the U.S. hard red winter wheat belt is likely to prompt USDA to boost its 1997 winter wheat production forecast.

The USDA wheat production and supply/demand reports will be released Friday at 0730 CDT. CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed unchanged to 5-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with July down 4-1/4 cents at $3.21-1/2 a bushel.
